title: Love your neighbor (Leviticus 19:9–18)
hook: leave the edges of the field for the poor; love your neighbor as yourself

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bezalel, the craftsman filled with the spirit of God for wisdom and workmanship. Your line: craft is spiritual.

A farmer is bringing in the harvest. The sickles swing through the wheat, row after row, and when they reach the corners of the field, they stop. On purpose. Behind them, a few stalks have fallen, and nobody goes back for them. In the vineyard, dropped grapes are left lying too. It looks like sloppy farming. It's actually the law, right in the middle of Leviticus, between the sacrifices, the skin diseases and the priestly clothing.
screen: `THE SICKLES STOP AT THE CORNERS.` → `THE FALLEN STALKS STAY DOWN.` → `IT'S THE LAW.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest." The grapes too: "thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger: I am the LORD your God." It's welfare built into the field itself. The poor don't beg at the farmhouse door. They walk in and gather what was left for them, with their own hands, with dignity. That's how Ruth, a poor foreign widow, ends up gleaning in the field of Boaz, a story the path reaches next year. The Jewish oral law later gave a whole tractate of the Mishnah to these corners, called Peah, corner. Then chapter nineteen keeps going, all ordinary life. Don't hold back a worker's wages overnight. "Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind." Don't spread gossip. Don't stand idle while your neighbor's life is in danger. Don't hate your brother in your heart, take revenge or bear a grudge. And then, almost tucked in at the end: "but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." This is the line Jesus will quote as the second great commandment, straight from Leviticus. Look at the shape of the chapter. Love your neighbor isn't a warm feeling floating in the air. It's corners of fields, wages paid on time, the deaf and the blind protected, grudges dropped. Love has edges you can see. And later in the same chapter, the stranger among you is to be loved as yourself too.
screen: `DON'T REAP THE CORNERS.` · `THE POOR GLEAN WITH DIGNITY.` · `NO GRUDGES, NO STUMBLING BLOCKS.` · `THE LINE JESUS WILL QUOTE.` · then, large: `“THOU SHALT LOVE THY NEIGHBOUR AS THYSELF.”`

segments.voice: Picture your own field: your paycheck, your pantry, your time, the last slice, the best seat. Choose one corner where you could stop the sickle a little early and leave something standing, without making a speech about it, and picture someone else gathering it. If you pray, pray for whoever will.
Peah. Hebrew for corner, the Mishnah's name for the harvest law: leaving the edges of the field standing for the poor and the stranger.
Your line: leave the edges. The field was built to feed more than the farmer. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians learn 'love thy neighbour as thyself' as the second great commandment, and some churches and farms practice modern gleaning, gathering leftover crops after harvest for food banks.

original.note: Hebrew: and you shall love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18).

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice saying from Jesus.
what it means: a line from Leviticus, at the end of a list of very concrete kindnesses: corners left, wages paid, grudges dropped.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 19:18, with 19:34 stretching it to the stranger; the corners became a whole Mishnah tractate, Peah.
recall: the bush that burned, not consumed

chat.says: Is "love your neighbor as yourself" something Jesus came up with?
options: He quoted Leviticus 19, where it follows laws on wages, grudges and field corners.
Yes, it first appears in the Gospels; the Old Testament never says it.
It comes from Proverbs, as a wise saying about being kind to friends.
chat.meaning: Love your neighbor as yourself is Leviticus 19:18, at the end of very concrete laws. Jesus quotes it as the second great commandment.

Peah.meaning: Hebrew for corner; the Mishnah's tractate on the harvest corners

Mishnah.meaning: the written collection of Jewish oral law

Boaz.meaning: the landowner in whose field Ruth gleaned

gleanings.meaning: stalks left fallen in the field for the poor to gather
